title: The Liver's hidden foe: A case study on Human Fasciolasis
case_text:
A man in his late twenties presented to the outpatient clinic with intermittent burning pain in the upper abdomen, both right and left quadrants, over the past year. He also reported nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, intermittent fever, and a weight loss of 7 kg. He had received multiple treatments for H. pylori gastritis in a clinic in his home town and underwent two upper GI endoscopies and the first one had a duodenal ulcer while the second one after the treatment of H.pylori with triple therapy (Omeprazole, Amoxicillin and Clarithromycin) was a healed doudenal ulcer. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and no abnormalities. Initial diagnosis included gastritis and consideration of a liver abscess, prompting blood work up, stool examination, and an abdominal ultrasound as shown in (Fig. 1) which recommended to have a contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan (Fig. 2). Incidental liver lesions on the abdominal ultrasound and CT scan prompted further investigation, including abdominal MRI with contrast and MRCP (Fig. 3) as well as serological tests for Fasciola hepatica and Toxocara.
The complete blood count, serum creatinine, ESR, and hsCRP levels were all within normal limits according to our laboratory standards. Urinalysis and stool examination did not show any abnormalities. Tests for HIV antibody, HBsAg, HCV antibody, and stool occult blood were negative. The stool antigen test for H. pylori was positive. .
The liver function tests showed a mildly elevated transaminases with elevated direct bilirubin and prolonged prothrombin time.
The serological tests confirmed the diagnosis of the Fasciola hepatica and oral triclabendazole as well as quadruple therapy (Pantoprazole, Metronidazole, Amoxicillin and Clarithromycin) for the H.pylori was prescribed.

distillation_prompt.system_prompt:
You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Foodborne Trematodes
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: Fasciola hepatica infection
